## Headline read — the most replicable thing

Kieren operates as a logistical orchestrator embedded in complex, multi-stakeholder projects rather than a traditional closer. His replicable habit is **structured handoff and clarity**: when a deal or project requires coordination across internal teams, landholders, or field partners, he documents relationships, flags dependencies, and explicitly assigns next steps (e.g., 'Do you need Carr or Tanner uploaded as priority? I will direct Michael accordingly.'). This eliminates ambiguity and keeps momentum alive in long-cycle agricultural projects.

## Discovery questions

- **Logistical / operational constraint clarification — Kieren asks 'what is feasible' or 'what is the priority' when coordinating field work or project sequencing.** — _surfaces:_ Physical constraints, scheduling conflicts, landholder preferences, and operational bandwidth. Surfaces what can actually be executed vs. what is theoretically desired.
  > "Do you need Carr or Tanner uploaded as priority? I will direct Michael accordingly. [2024-10-18, Andrew Yates]"
  > "Can you let me know the relationship. They seem to be a long way apart. Will try and organise both but logistically does not make sense. [2024-10-18, Andrew Yates response]"
- **Contact / relationship mapping — when inheriting a project or deal, Kieren asks for or clarifies who the key stakeholder is and how they are connected to other projects or phases.** — _surfaces:_ Identifies whether a contact is a primary decision-maker, a coordinator, or a field executor; clarifies whether multiple projects can be bundled or must be separated.
  > "I hadn't actually clocked that they were not geographically close. [2024-10-18, acknowledging prior knowledge gap about Carr vs. Tanner geography]"
  > "Bill looped you in on the relationships. [2024-10-18, to Andrew Yates, assuming prior context-setting]"
- **Capability / capacity check — Kieren asks internal or external partners whether they have bandwidth or readiness to execute next phases (e.g., data upload, account setup).** — _surfaces:_ Prevents over-committing and ensures customer onboarding is staged correctly.
  > "can we push our run-through of the software out by a week so I can set up your account properly? Sorry for the delay [2024-03-27, Adam Rabjohns]"

## Transitions

### From initial contact / discovery → technical / operational setup phase

Kieren signals readiness to move to hands-on execution by proposing a structured onboarding or meeting agenda, often involving his team and the customer's requirements in parallel.

> "In this session Dylan and I will set you up with: Your own Ceres Portal Transfer the tags from our AgriProve Ceres portal to yours Register you for the AgriProve software Link your Ceres Tags to the AgriProve software [2024-04-08, Adam Rabjohns onboarding]"
> "Please find attached the draft sampling plans for your carbon project. Can you please review this plan with the following questions in mind: Are all project areas included? [2024-03-28, Justin Costello, discovery → sampling plan delivery]"

### From approval / decision gate → field execution / coordination

Once a customer confirms or a logistical decision is made, Kieren immediately directs internal teams ('I will direct Michael accordingly') and confirms next step with the customer or field partner.

> "Apologies, I hadn't actually clocked that they were not geographically close. Do you need Carr or Tanner uploaded as priority? I will direct Michael accordingly. [2024-10-18]"
> "Contact Tony as below - I believe Bill looped you in on the relationships. [2024-10-18, clarifying who will manage the next phase]"

### From project execution / field work → customer relationship maintenance / follow-up

After a major milestone or visit, Kieren consolidates the interaction (e.g., sending updated results maps, clarifying technical methodology) and signals future engagement.

> "Lovely to meet you in person a couple of weeks ago, thanks again for having us. Please see attached your updated results maps for the RMIT project sampling. [2024-04-25, Adam Rabjohns, post-visit follow-up]"
> "We have included the points so you can see how this method has extrapolated over the broader area. We also get a lot of questions on the moisture vs gravimetric water tests [technical clarity on methodology]"

## Customer archetypes — who they engaged well

### The Large-Scale Regenerative Operator (innovator / thought leader)

**Characteristics.** Multi-thousand hectare farms, implementing advanced grazing techniques, high capital investment in infrastructure, operationally sophisticated, willing to adopt new tools/methodologies, sees data as competitive advantage.

**Approach.** Position as case study / reference. Invest time in understanding their operational constraints (labour, logistics, animal density). Document and reference their innovation back to them. Offer customized solutions (e.g., adapted sampling schedules) rather than one-size-fits-all. Engage at the operational level (GM, owner) and foster ongoing thought partnership.

**Example.** Adam Rabjohns (General Manager, 52 engagements): Kieren hosted him + hosted him for a ministerial visit. Noted his sophisticated grazing management (3x daily moves, 420 head/ha, strip grazing). Offered alternatives (gifting OptiWeigh elsewhere) when he changed needs. Continued engagement despite product non-use.

### The Project Coordinator / Field Partner (intermediary)

**Characteristics.** Land resource specialist, environmental consultant, or field operations manager. Acts as interface between AgriProve and landholders. Manages field logistics and timing. Has strong opinions on feasibility. Prefers clarity over sales pressure.

**Approach.** Ask them 'what is feasible?' first, then work backward. Respect their constraints (geography, landholder availability, scheduling). Provide them with internal contact info and make it clear you will re-prioritize based on their input. Acknowledge when you've missed a detail ('I hadn't actually clocked that they were not geographically close'). Frame your flexibility as a feature, not a concession.

**Example.** Andrew Yates (Land Resource Specialist, Verterra, 60 engagements): Flagged that Carr and Tanner projects were geographically too far apart to sequence together. Kieren did not push back; instead asked 'Do you need Carr or Tanner uploaded as priority?' Andrew then called the landholder, got a preference (Tanner), and confirmed timing. Deal accelerated, no friction.

### The Customer in Ongoing Relationship / Lifecycle Phase (product user)

**Characteristics.** Already deployed AgriProve's software or sampling service. Now managing ongoing use, results interpretation, or renewal. May have operational changes that affect product fit. Values technical transparency and relationship continuity.

**Approach.** Bundle technical clarity (explain methodology, address FAQ questions proactively) with operational listening (note changes in their business). Use deliverables (results maps, updated data) as touchpoints. Frame changes in their needs (e.g., product non-use) as intelligence, not failures. Keep them engaged as reference customers or thought partners even if a specific product is no longer in use.

**Example.** Justin Costello (customer, 74 engagements): Multi-year engagement spanning 2023–2026. Started with data visualization meetings (2023-12), progressed through documentation (2024-01), sampling plan reviews (2024-03–04), and morphed into ongoing project status calls and platform feedback (2026-04). Kieren's team (Dylan Cronje) handled 2026 call with casual tone ('teasing Dylan about retirement'), indicating warm relationship.

### The Prospective Large-Scale Project Partner (long-cycle deal)

**Characteristics.** Interested in large regenerative grazing or carbon farming projects (e.g., 20k ha GC LRF project). May involve multiple stakeholders, funding, regulatory approval. Slow decision cycle but high deal size. Requires relationship-building and repeated touchpoints.

**Approach.** Pass relevant materials (CTR/CTI = likely case studies or technical references). Call to confirm interest. Ask about decision-making (who else needs to be looped in, e.g., 'he said he will talk to GC about LRF project'). Schedule repeated check-ins via phone. Don't over-pitch; let the scale and quality of the opportunity speak. Patience + gentle re-engagement.

**Example.** Wayne Hanrahan (80 engagements, 2022–2026): 8000 ha cattle operation involved in a 20k ha Queensland GC LRF project. Kieren passed materials (CTR/CTI, 2022-01-20), left a message (2022-01-19), confirmed Wayne would loop in the main project stakeholder (GC). Then multiple phone calls spanning 2025–2026, including a wind turbine discussion. No clear close yet, but relationship maintained for 4+ years—consistent with long-cycle agricultural projects.

## Anti-patterns visible

- **Heavy reliance on email summaries and handoff notes rather than direct customer conversation for major decisions. Many of Kieren's key coordination moves (priority calls, project sequencing) are communicated via email or internal notes rather than confirmed via direct conversation.** — 2024-10-18 Verterra coordination thread: Kieren emails Andrew Yates asking 'Do you need Carr or Tanner uploaded as priority?' Andrew then responds via email, Kieren then directs Michael via email. No recorded call between Kieren and Andrew during this decision gate. A direct 10-minute call would have been faster and reduced ambiguity.
- **Limited visible objection handling or reframing of customer concerns beyond logistics. The corpus shows Kieren accommodating constraints (geography, labour, scheduling) but does not show him challenging or reframing a customer's underlying belief or hesitation about the product itself.** — Adam Rabjohns stopped using the OptiWeigh unit due to labour constraints ('can't keep up with the labour requirements to move that frequently'). Kieren documented this and offered to gift it elsewhere. No record of Kieren suggesting a scaled version, a different tool, or a labour-saving workaround. The pivoting to reference customer / thought partner is smart, but it is not objection *handling*—it is objection *acceptance*.
- **Frequent re-scheduling and delays in customer-facing deliverables, though always with explanation and apology. Multiple instances of 'Sorry for the delay' or 'Apologies' when pushing back meeting dates or bumping emails.** — 2024-03-27: 'can we push our run-through of the software out by a week so I can set up your account properly? Sorry for the delay',2024-04-04: 'Bumping this email for approval of the Draft Sample Plan to continue with finalising the sample locations for the field technicians. Please respond to this email with confirmation at your earliest convenience.',2023-04-21: multiple back-and-forths on T1 Sampling Plans, with delays in clarifying sampling method questions.
